function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish the whole workflow.  
I’ve also included the exact file contents you’ll need to add to the repo.

> **⚠️ Important** – I can’t actually clone the repo or push commits for you, but the commands below will do it for you on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & create artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

> The repo is a simple Node.js app that listens on port **3000** (check `package.json` or `app.js`).  
> We’ll use the lightweight `node:18-alpine` image.

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small and production‑ready.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean install from `package-lock.json`.  
> * Exposing port 3000 matches the app’s listening port.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

> We’ll create a **Deployment** (2 replicas) and a **Service** (ClusterIP) that forwards traffic to the pods on port 3000.

Create a file named `k8s-deployment.yaml` in the repo root:

```yaml
# k8s-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- change if you use another registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Pod port
```

> **Tip** – If you’re using Docker Hub instead of GitHub Container Registry, replace the image URL accordingly.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

> Build the Docker image, push it to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR), and optionally deploy to a cluster (if you have a `kubectl` context set).

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write   # Needed to push to GHCR

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: |
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      # Optional: Deploy to a cluster (uncomment if you have a kubeconfig secret)
      # - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      #   uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
      #   with:
      #     manifests: k8s-deployment.yaml
      #     images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What this workflow does**  
> 1. Checks out the repo.  
> 2. Builds the Docker image using the Dockerfile.  
> 3. Pushes two tags: `latest` and the commit SHA.  
> 4. (Optional) Deploys to a Kubernetes cluster if you enable the commented section.

---

## 3️⃣ Add, commit, and push the new files

```bash
# Stage the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s-deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to main
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run on the `main` branch, building and publishing the Docker image.

---

## 4️⃣ Verify

1. **Check the Actions tab** – you should see a successful run.  
2. **Pull the image** (optional):

   ```bash
   docker pull ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
   ```

3. **Deploy to a cluster** (if you have one):

   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s-deployment.yaml
   ```

   Then expose the service via `kubectl port-forward svc/nodejs-welcome-service 8080:80` and visit `http://localhost:8080`.

---

### 🎉 Done!

You now have:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s-deployment.yaml` | Deployment + Service for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline that builds & pushes the image |

Feel free to tweak the image registry, tags, or deployment details to fit your environment. Happy coding!
